title: Full Multiparty System Restored
reason: Country, year, and several core facts check out: Senghor did amend the constitution in 1976 (Law 76-01 of March 19, 1976), the ruling UPS was renamed Parti Socialiste (PS) that year, and Abdoulaye Wade's PDS was legally recognized under the new law. However, the event's central characterization is materially wrong: this was NOT a restoration of "full multiparty competition" with restrictions removed. Law 76-01 explicitly restricted legal political activity to exactly three parties, each required to represent one of three predefined ideological 'tendencies' (socialist/social-democrat = PS, liberal/democrat = PDS, Marxist-Leninist = PAI, legalized Aug 1976). A fourth tendency (conservative) was added in 1978 (Law 78-60). Unrestricted multiparty competition — any citizen free to form a party — was only established later, by Law 81-17 of May 6, 1981, under Abdou Diouf. So the 'full multiparty' / 'removed restrictions' framing describes 1981, not 1976; 1976 was a limited/managed three-tendency liberalization. This is a scope/magnitude error material to the event's title and thrust, while year, country, and the PS/PDS details hold — hence PARTIAL, not TRUE.

title: Senegal Liquidates Seven State-Linked Banks After Systemic Insolvency

Senegal led the coalition force (with Nigeria, Mali, Togo, Ghana) that entered Gambia on Jan 19, 2017; Jammeh stepped down and left the country Jan 21, 2017. In 2014, the only Gambia-related incident was an unrelated failed coup attempt (Dec 30, 2014) by gunmen allegedly transiting via Senegal — there was no ECOWAS force, no Barrow election crisis, and no Senegalese-led regional military mission against Gambia that year. The year is materially wrong, so the event as dated is false.

The event described — Senegal leading/joining an ECOWAS force to confront a Gambian political crisis under Yahya Jammeh (troops massing, hosting exiles, economic pressure to force him from power) — is the well-documented ECOWAS military intervention in The Gambia (Operation Restore Democracy / ECOMIG), which took place in January 2017, after Jammeh refused to accept his December 2016 election loss to Adama Barrow. Senegalese troops entered Gambia on 19 January 2017 at Barrow's request; Jammeh departed 21 January 2017. Nothing matching this description occurred in 2014. The only Gambia-related event in 2014 was a failed coup attempt against Jammeh (30 December 2014) staged by plotters who entered FROM Senegal — the opposite framing (Senegalese territory used against Jammeh by private plotters, not an ECOWAS force joining a coalition against him), and no ECOWAS force or Senegalese-led coalition action occurred that year. The description's added detail about Senegal's role in the ECOWAS Mission in Guinea-Bissau (ECOMIB, est. 2012) is a separate, unrelated mission conflated into this entry. Year and substance both indicate this is a real event mis-dated by three years.

title: Senegal Bans Single-Use Plastics Nationwide
reason: Law No. 2020-04 (voted Jan 8, 2020), banning production/import/sale of single-use plastics (bags, straws, cups), took effect in Senegal on April 20, 2020, confirmed by phys.org, Greenpeace Africa, and allAfrica. It repeals/builds on the 2015 plastic bag law (Law No. 2015-09) that was barely enforced (phys.org, elaw.org). French-language sources (pfongue.org citing the Heinrich Böll Stiftung legal analysis) confirm the law establishes a deposit-return (consigne) system for plastic bottles (Articles 6-14) and an extended producer responsibility (REP) scheme (Article 11). The COVID-19 exception allowing continued sale of plastic water sachets is explicitly confirmed by Greenpeace Africa, phys.org, and allAfrica, quoting Environment Minister Abdou Karim Sall. All material details (country, year, effective date, 2015 precursor, deposit-return system, EPR, sachet exception) are corroborated by multiple independent sources.
